content: 1. The study by Eshun-Wilson et al. (2005) explored the phenomenon of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in AIDS patients with Cryptococcus neoformans infection during the era of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). It was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2. Eshun-Wilson et al. (2018) compared early versus delayed initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in HIV-positive individuals with cryptococcal meningitis. This systematic review is currently in press in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 3. Bisson et al. (2013) investigated the impact of early versus delayed ART initiation on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) fungal clearance in adults with HIV and cryptococcal meningitis. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 4. Boulware et al. (2014) examined the timing of ART initiation following a diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis. Their study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, provided critical insights into the optimal timing of ART in this context. 5. Makadzange et al. (2010) conducted a study in sub-Saharan Africa to evaluate early versus delayed ART initiation in patients with concurrent HIV infection and cryptococcal meningitis. The results were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 6. Zolopa et al. (2009) demonstrated that early ART initiation reduces AIDS progression and mortality in individuals with acute opportunistic infections. This multicenter randomized trial was published in PLoS One. 7. Bicanic et al. (2007) assessed fungal burden, early fungicidal activity, and outcomes in cryptococcal meningitis patients treated with amphotericin B or fluconazole. Their study, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, included both ART-naïve and ART-experienced patients. 8. The Southern African HIV Clinicians Society (2013) released updated guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis, and management of cryptococcal meningitis in HIV-infected individuals. These guidelines were published in the South African Journal of HIV Medicine. 9. Aberg et al. (2002) conducted a pilot study on discontinuing antifungal therapy for disseminated cryptococcal disease in AIDS patients who achieved immunologic recovery with ART. The findings were published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases. 10. Kirk et al. (2002) evaluated the safe interruption of maintenance therapy for four common HIV-associated opportunistic infections during potent ART. Their study was published in the Annals of Internal Medicine. 11. Martínez et al. (2000) investigated the discontinuation of secondary prophylaxis for cryptococcal meningitis in HIV-infected patients responding to HAART. The results were published in AIDS. 12. Mussini et al. (2004) conducted an international observational study on discontinuing maintenance therapy for cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS patients treated with HAART. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 13. Rollot et al. (2001) examined the discontinuation of secondary prophylaxis against cryptococcosis in AIDS patients receiving HAART. The study was published in AIDS. 14. Sheng et al. (2002) reported successful discontinuation of fluconazole as secondary prophylaxis for cryptococcosis in AIDS patients responding to HAART. Their findings were published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS. 15. Vibhagool et al. (2003) conducted a prospective, multicenter, randomized study on discontinuing secondary prophylaxis for cryptococcal meningitis in HIV-infected patients treated with HAART. The results were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 16. The WHO guidelines for the diagnosis, prevention, and management of cryptococcal disease in HIV-infected adults, adolescents, and children were updated in 2017. These guidelines emphasize the use of serum or plasma cryptococcal antigen screening, pre-emptive antifungal therapy, and phased antifungal treatment regimens. 17. The WHO guideline development process involved systematic evidence synthesis, virtual and in-person meetings, and adherence to the GRADE methodology to assess evidence quality and recommendation strength. Peer review and conflict of interest management were integral to the process. 18. Diagnostic assays for cryptococcal disease, including CSF latex agglutination, lateral-flow assays, and enzyme immunoassays, were evaluated for sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. Lateral-flow assays demonstrated excellent performance, particularly in serum and plasma, but showed poor diagnostic accuracy in urine. 19. Limited data exist on the performance of diagnostic tests for isolated pulmonary cryptococcal disease. For non-meningeal and non-pulmonary cryptococcal disease, serum or plasma antigen testing can be used alongside histopathological examination and culture of appropriate samples. 20. The WHO guidelines also address the feasibility and acceptability of cryptococcal antigen screening and pre-emptive fluconazole therapy, particularly in resource-limited settings. These strategies were informed by surveys and consultations with healthcare providers and stakeholders. 21. The guideline development group ensured transparency and minimized conflicts of interest by excluding members with significant competing interests from voting on specific recommendations. External peer review and public consultation further strengthened the guideline development process.
